title: Review: Oxidative phosphorylation and chemiosmosis; Light-dependent reactions; Respiration overview and glycolysis
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PS02a#t2 term and clue written for the game; RS01#t2 term and clue written for the game; RS03b#t4 term and clue written for the game; PS02a#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: PS02a#N.12a, PS02b#N.5, RS01#N.9a, RS03b#N.9a, PS02a#N.8, PS02b#N.2, RS01#N.10, RS03b#N.4a, PS02a#N.4a, RS01#N.2a, PS02a#N.7a, RS01#N.12b. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Photophosphorylation
items.clue: Name for making ATP in thylakoids using energy that came from light.

items.label: Glycolysis
items.clue: First stage: glucose is converted to 2 pyruvate in the cytoplasm, with no oxygen needed.

items.label: Thylakoid space
items.clue: The lumen: the compartment into which H⁺ are pumped using energy from excited electrons.

items.label: Chemiosmosis
items.clue: Mechanism in which H⁺ flowing down their gradient through a synthase drive ATP formation.

questions.stem: A chemical is added that takes electrons from photosystem I in place of NADP. The chloroplasts are illuminated with a supply of water, ADP, phosphate and NADP. Which prediction is correct?

options.text: ATP synthesis stops, because ATP is made only when electrons reach NADP.
Oxygen release stops, because water is split only when NADP is being reduced.
Oxygen is still released and ATP still made, but no reduced NADP forms.
Everything stops, because the photosystems need reduced NADP before they can emit electrons.

questions.explanation: Electrons still flow from water through PSII, the chain and PSI, so photolysis and proton pumping continue. Only the final acceptor has changed.

questions.stem: A herbicide blocks the flow of electrons out of photosystem II. Chloroplasts treated with it are kept in bright light with a supply of ADP, phosphate and NADP. Which process can continue?

options.text: Oxygen release, because light continues to split water molecules directly whether or not photosystem II passes on its electrons.
Continuous reduction of NADP, because photosystem I generates its own electrons from light and so needs no supply from elsewhere.
No ATP production at all, because both the cyclic and the non-cyclic pathways begin with electrons emitted by photosystem II.
ATP production by cyclic photophosphorylation, since photosystem I can still emit electrons that return to it via the carriers.

questions.stem: During glycolysis of one glucose molecule, two ATP are used in phosphorylation and four ATP are formed later. What is the net yield per glucose?

options.text: A net gain of 2 ATP together with 2 reduced NAD
A net gain of 4 ATP as well as 2 reduced NAD
A net gain of 6 ATP plus another 2 reduced NAD
A net gain of 2 ATP together with 2 oxidised NAD

questions.explanation: Four formed minus two used gives two ATP. The oxidation steps also give two reduced NAD, and two pyruvate form.

questions.stem: A chemical is added that makes the thylakoid membrane freely permeable to protons, so that no proton gradient can build up across it. The chloroplasts are illuminated with a supply of ADP, phosphate and NADP. Which prediction is correct?

options.text: ATP is still made, because the electron carriers phosphorylate ADP directly as the electrons pass along.
Oxygen and reduced NADP continue to be produced in the light, but ATP synthesis stops completely.
Everything stops, because without ATP the photosystems have no energy to emit electrons.
More ATP is made, because the protons now reach ATP synthase in the stroma more quickly than before.

questions.stem: In illuminated chloroplasts of a hypothetical alga, the pH of the thylakoid space was 5.0 and the pH of the stroma was 8.0. What is the H⁺ concentration in the thylakoid space as a multiple of the H⁺ concentration in the stroma?

options.text: 3 times
1000 times
30 times
0.001 times

questions.explanation: Each pH unit is a tenfold difference. The thylakoid space is 3.0 units lower, so its H⁺ concentration is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 times greater: a steep gradient built by electron transport.

questions.stem: Why is a structured array of many different pigment molecules, rather than a single chlorophyll molecule, needed to carry out the first step of photosynthesis?

options.text: Different pigments absorb a wide range of wavelengths and funnel the energy to one reaction centre, which is excited far more often than a lone molecule.
Each pigment molecule in the array carries out photosynthesis by itself, so the array simply packs more independent working units into the thylakoid membrane.
The accessory pigments only protect the chlorophyll from damage by bright light; a single chlorophyll could absorb the light equally well by itself.
Every pigment in the array emits its own excited electron to the electron carriers, so the array releases many more electrons per second than one molecule would.

questions.stem: In one reaction of the Krebs cycle, two hydrogen atoms (each with an electron) are removed from a substrate and accepted by NAD. Which statement describes this reaction?

options.text: The substrate is reduced and NAD is oxidised by the transfer.
Neither substance is oxidised, because no oxygen takes part in it.
The substrate has been oxidised and NAD has been reduced.
The substrate is oxidised, but NAD only holds hydrogen and is unchanged.

questions.explanation: Removing hydrogen with its electron oxidises the substrate; NAD, which accepts it, is reduced. The two happen together as a redox reaction.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how ATP is produced in the thylakoid?

options.text: Reduced NADP passes its electrons to the carriers, which pump protons for ATP synthesis, exactly as reduced NAD does in mitochondria.
The electron carriers make ATP directly as electrons pass along them, transferring the energy of each electron into a phosphate bond on ADP.
Protons are pumped out of the lumen into the stroma and flow back into the lumen through ATP synthase, releasing ATP inside it.
Electron carriers pump protons into the thylakoid lumen, and the protons flow back into the stroma through ATP synthase, which makes ATP.

questions.explanation: Energy from excited electrons passing along the carriers pumps protons into the lumen; ATP synthase uses their flow back into the stroma to phosphorylate ADP.

questions.stem: Which statement about the photolysis of water in photosystem II is correct?

options.text: Light absorbed directly by water molecules in the thylakoid lumen breaks them apart into hydrogen gas and oxygen gas.
The hydrogen released from water is passed straight to NADP at photosystem II, reducing it before the electrons move on.
Its electrons replace those lost by the reaction centre, its protons join the gradient and oxygen is waste.
Oxygen is the useful product of photolysis, and the protons and electrons are waste that diffuses out of the chloroplast.

questions.explanation: Photolysis yields electrons, which replace those emitted by the reaction-centre chlorophyll, and protons, released into the thylakoid lumen. The oxygen is a waste product that diffuses away.

questions.stem: Which organisms release energy by the oxidation of carbon compounds in cell respiration?

options.text: Heterotrophs at all times, but autotrophs only at night, when they cannot obtain energy from photosynthesis.
All autotrophs and all heterotrophs, in every living cell, throughout the day and the night.
Only organisms with lungs or gills, because respiration depends on breathing to take in oxygen from the air or water.
Heterotrophs and chemoautotrophs only, because photoautotrophs use light rather than oxidation as their energy source.

questions.explanation: Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals all respire continuously. Photosynthesis in autotrophs is an extra process, not a replacement.

questions.stem: Which processes in an illuminated chloroplast build up the proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane?

options.text: Electron transport chain pumping, photolysis inside the thylakoid, and NADP reduction in the stroma
Only pumping by the electron transport chain, since photolysis releases its protons into the stroma
ATP synthase, which uses ATP to pump protons from the stroma into the thylakoid space
Reducing NADP, which releases protons into the thylakoid space

questions.explanation: All three raise [H⁺] inside the thylakoid relative to the stroma: two add H⁺ inside, one removes H⁺ outside.

questions.stem: Aerobic respiration of one glucose molecule yields many times more ATP than anaerobic respiration (2). Which statement explains the difference?

options.text: Both pathways run in the mitochondria, but without oxygen the mitochondria work more slowly and so make less ATP.
Without oxygen the cell uses the little oxygen dissolved in its cytoplasm, so only a small amount of ATP forms.
Without oxygen the cell converts glucose to ethanol, which keeps most of the energy, so much less ATP is made.
Without oxygen only glycolysis in the cytoplasm yields ATP; with oxygen the mitochondria release far more of the energy in glucose.
